principles.text: Talk to users in person: 20-30 conversations tell you more than 10,000 signups from Google Ads.
Before PMF, skip graphs and growth hacking. Get 1, then 10, then 100 users who love the product.
Pivot when you're out of growth ideas, and move closer to what you're an expert in.
Create more value than you capture. If your retention is bad, you are not creating value.
Spend aggressively only into a channel that proves it pays back; otherwise bank the money.

sampleQA.question: How do I know when to pivot?

answer.text: Pivot when you're out of ideas to make it grow. If you still have many untried ones, stay the course.
Beware the uncanny valley of PMF: a little traction keeps you stuck, while a total failure lets you move on.
Don't confuse customer politeness with traction.
A good pivot gets warmer toward your expertise and builds on what you learned from the last idea.

sampleQA.question: Should my product be free and ad-supported or paid?

answer.text: If a service is too important to its users, charge for it. A paid, profitable steward builds a better product.
Free with a vague model is a trap: costs balloon with growth, forcing a sale, ads or endless fundraising.
Pricing high can signal a real insight. Stripe was the most expensive option and people still wanted it.

sampleQA.question: How should I approach raising my Series A?

answer.text: Win with growth and proof points, not deck polish.
Fundraising is a distraction. Do it in as little time as possible.
Ask investors how many deals they did last year and call those founders. The slowest investors have the worst returns.
Avoid a bloated seed followed by an A six months later that sells 15-20%.
